CausalChain: Chronic metabolic stress (NAFLD/obesity) → Enhanced de novo lipogenesis → Increased saturated fatty acids production → Shift in ceramide profile (increased C16-ceramide, decreased polyunsaturated species) → Impaired p53-mediated apoptotic signaling and enhanced NF-κB activation → Dysregulated bile acid signaling further amplifies inflammatory cytokine production → Creation of an immune suppressive, pro-tumorigenic microenvironment → Promotion of hepatocellular carcinoma development.
Hypothesis: A shift in ceramide species—marked by an increase in saturated C16-ceramide combined with dysregulated bile acid signaling—creates a pro-inflammatory, immunosuppressive microenvironment that drives the initiation and progression of hepatocellular carcinoma. Restoring a balanced ceramide profile may reactivate apoptotic pathways and improve tumor immune surveillance.
Abstract: The liver‐cancer microenvironment is shaped by a complex interplay between lipid metabolic reprogramming and inflammatory signaling. In conditions such as non‐alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and obesity, enhanced de novo lipogenesis drives not only lipid accumulation but also alters the composition of bioactive lipids that serve as both structural components and signaling molecules. Changes in sphingolipid metabolism, particularly a shift from polyunsaturated ceramide species to increased levels of saturated C16‐ceramide, coupled with dysregulated bile acid synthesis, may suppress tumor suppressor pathways (for example, p53 activation) and upregulate NF‐κB–mediated inflammatory cascades. This perturbation appears to disrupt immune surveillance and foster an environment conducive to tumor initiation and progression. In this context, modulating the balance of ceramide species offers a potential therapeutic avenue to restore apoptotic sensitivity and reinvigorate antitumor immunity.
